clinicalPearls: NIHL results from prolonged exposure to hazardous noise and is typically bilateral, symmetrical and sensorineural
The audiogram classically shows a notch at around 4 kHz that later broadens to involve neighbouring frequencies as damage progresses
Both the sound intensity and the cumulative duration of exposure determine risk, and damage accumulates over years of work
Early loss is often unnoticed because speech frequencies are relatively spared at first, and tinnitus may be the first complaint
A temporary threshold shift after a noisy shift can recover, but repeated insults lead to permanent threshold shift
The loss is irreversible once established, so prevention through noise control, hearing protection and audiometric surveillance is paramount
Presbyacusis and other causes of sensorineural loss must be considered, especially in older workers, and the exposure history is central to attribution
Impulse or blast noise can cause acute acoustic trauma, sometimes with sudden asymmetric loss or eardrum rupture
reference.pathophysiology: Excessive acoustic energy causes mechanical and metabolic injury to the outer hair cells of the cochlea, initially at the basal turn that encodes higher frequencies around 3 to 6 kHz. Repeated exposure produces oxidative stress and progressive, irreversible hair cell loss, giving a sensorineural deficit that begins as the characteristic high-frequency notch and widens with continued exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Conductive loss from middle ear disease or wax
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Pure tone audiometry to characterise the notch and threshold shifts
Occupational noise exposure history and workplace noise measurements
Comparison with baseline and serial surveillance audiograms
Referral for imaging if hearing loss is markedly asymmetric to exclude retrocochlear pathology
redFlags: Sudden or markedly asymmetric sensorineural loss requiring urgent evaluation
Unilateral tinnitus or loss suggesting acoustic neuroma
Acute acoustic trauma with pain, vertigo or tympanic membrane rupture
Rapidly progressive loss inconsistent with noise exposure alone
reference.prognosis: Established noise-induced loss does not recover and there is no curative treatment; however, further deterioration can be halted by removing or controlling exposure, and communication is aided by hearing devices, making prevention the decisive factor.
pitfalls: Assuming all hearing loss in older workers is age-related and missing a noise contribution
Overlooking asymmetry that should prompt investigation for tumour
Relying on a single audiogram rather than serial surveillance
Neglecting to enforce hearing protection and noise control at source
management: Prevent further irreversible injury through workplace noise control — engineering source reduction and enclosure, administrative limits on exposure time, and consistently worn earplugs or earmuffs
Fit and optimise hearing aids for the established sensorineural loss, with assistive listening devices and aural rehabilitation to support communication
Provide tinnitus support such as sound therapy and counselling, as tinnitus is often the presenting complaint
Undertake serial audiometric surveillance compared with baseline to detect early threshold shift and reinforce protective measures
Refer for cochlear implant assessment when loss becomes severe to profound and amplification no longer suffices
Arrange neuro-imaging and otology referral for markedly asymmetric loss to exclude retrocochlear pathology
Coordinate occupational health review for exposure reassessment, redeployment away from hazardous noise, and statutory reporting
